1.note: Isaiah is using the word **Woe** to express his distress about what will happen to the people of Ephraim. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Disaster is coming to]

Isaiah is speaking as if the city of Samaria were **the crown of the pride of the drunkards of Ephraim**. He means that Samaria sits on a hilltop above the fertile valley like a crown on the head of a drunken person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the city that the drunkards of Ephraim are proud of]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the boasting of]

Isaiah is speaking as if the beauty of Samaria were **the fading flower**. He means that the beauty and prosperity of the city will soon pass away. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [yes, {to} the splendor of its beauty that is fading away]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **splendor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [splendid in]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **beauty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how beautiful it looks]
The pronoun **its** refers to the city of Samaria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Samaria’s beauty]

Isaiah is speaking as if the hilltop location of Samaria were **the head** of the rich valley below it. He means that the city sits prominently above a valley known for its fertile abundance. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the top of a fertile valley]

The expression **the ones overcome** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to those whom wine has overcome]

Isaiah is using the participle **the ones overcome** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to those who have drunk too much wine]

2.note: Isaiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Know this!]

2.q: כְּ⁠זֶ֥רֶם בָּרָ֖ד שַׂ֣עַר קָ֑טֶב כְּ֠⁠זֶרֶם מַ֣יִם כַּבִּירִ֥ים שֹׁטְפִ֛ים
2.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a storm of hail** and **a storm of mighty, overflowing waters** are powerful and destructive, so the one whom Yahweh sends against Ephraim will be powerful and destructive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as a storm of hail and a storm of mighty, overflowing waters are powerful and destructive]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **windstorm** that is characterized by **destruction**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a destructive windstorm]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [tearing everything down]

Isaiah is using the word **hand** to mean the power of the one whom Yahweh sends, since hands are used to exert power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by his power]
The pronoun **he** refers to the mighty one whom Yahweh sends against Ephraim. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that mighty one casts {it} down]

3.note: Isaiah is using the feminine plural verbal form **they will be trampled** when the subject is feminine singular, **the crown**. Interpreters are not certain why he uses the plural. This could be by attraction to the preceding feminine plural (dual) indirect object **feet**. Express this in the way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [it will be trampled]

The expression **they will be trampled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will trample it]

The pronoun **they** refers to the crown of the pride of the drunkards of Ephraim, that is, the people of Samaria and their glory. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Samaria will be trampled]
See how you translated the similar expression in [28:1](ta:28).

Isaiah is using one part of the body, **feet**, to mean the whole person who walks. He means that people will trample the crown of the pride of the drunkards of Ephraim. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [By those who step on them]

4.q: וְֽ⁠הָ֨יְתָ֜ה צִיצַ֤ת נֹבֵל֙ צְבִ֣י תִפְאַרְתּ֔⁠וֹ אֲשֶׁ֥ר עַל רֹ֖אשׁ גֵּ֣יא שְׁמָנִ֑ים כְּ⁠בִכּוּרָהּ֙ בְּ⁠טֶ֣רֶם קַ֔יִץ
4.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a firstfruit before the summer harvest** is quickly snatched up and eaten as soon as someone sees it, so the fading beauty of Samaria will be quickly consumed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And the fading flower, the splendor of its beauty, which {is} on the head of a valley of fatnesses, will be quickly consumed, like a firstfruit before summer]
See how you translated the similar expression in [28:1](ta:28).
See how you translated the similar expression in [28:1](ta:28).
The pronoun **it** refers to the firstfruit fig. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the fig]

5.note: SPEAKER is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [text]

He means that Yahweh himself will be the source of honor and glory for the faithful remnant of Israel. If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **beauty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a beautiful diadem]

6.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [right decisions]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [deciding cases]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and strengthens]

7.note: Isaiah uses the words **And these also** to indicate a contrast between the future glory that Yahweh will be for his faithful remnant and the present condition of the priests and prophets, who stagger with drunkenness. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But these also]
The pronoun **these** refers to the priests and prophets of Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these priests and prophets]

Isaiah is using the two terms **wine** and **beer** together to mean all kinds of alcoholic drinks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with all kinds of alcoholic drinks … with all kinds of alcoholic drinks … with all kinds of alcoholic drinks]
The pronoun **they** refers to the priest and prophet. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these two reel]

Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are overcome by wine]

Isaiah is speaking as if the priests and prophets literally **stagger** and **stumble** when they try to see visions and make judgments. 8.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for the drunken errors of the priests and prophets described in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because]

Isaiah is saying **all tables** as a generalization for emphasis. He does not necessarily mean every table without exception but rather that vomit and filth are widespread. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [tables everywhere]

9.q: אֶת מִי֙ יוֹרֶ֣ה דֵעָ֔ה וְ⁠אֶת מִ֖י
9.note: This is the beginning of what the drunken leaders say in mockery. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a quotation.

The pronoun **he** refers to Isaiah. The drunken leaders are mocking him by asking who he thinks he can teach. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will Isaiah teach]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he knows]

Isaiah is using the question form to continue the contemptuous mockery of the drunken leaders. They suggest that his teaching is only fit for small children. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is as though we were babies just weaned from milk and withdrawn from the breasts!]

The expression **the ones withdrawn** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones their mothers have weaned]

9.q: אֶת מִי֙ יוֹרֶ֣ה דֵעָ֔ה וְ⁠אֶת מִ֖י יָבִ֣ין שְׁמוּעָ֑ה
9.note: Isaiah is using the question form to express the mocking contempt of the drunken leaders. They imply that they do not need God’s teaching, delivered to them by Isaiah. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [As if he could teach us knowledge, or make us understand the report!]

The expressions **The ones weaned** and **the ones withdrawn** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Those who have stopped drinking milk, the ones their mothers have weaned]

10.q: צַ֤ו לָ⁠צָו֙ צַ֣ו לָ⁠צָ֔ו קַ֥ו לָ⁠קָ֖ו קַ֣ו לָ⁠קָ֑ו זְעֵ֥יר שָׁ֖ם זְעֵ֥יר שָֽׁם
10.note: The drunken leaders are repeating **command by command, command by command, line by line, line by line** as a mocking imitation of what they consider to be Isaiah’s tedious, overly simplistic teaching. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this irony in another way. Alternate translation: [it is nothing but command by command, command by command, line by line, line by line, a little here, a little there]

This is the end of what the drunken leaders say in mockery. You may wish to mark the end of this speech with a closing quotation mark or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate the end of a quotation.

11.note: Isaiah is using the word **lip** to mean a foreign language, since lips are used to speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the stammering speech of a foreign language]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **stammerings** that are characterized by being from a foreign **lip**, that is, speech that sounds like stammering because it is in a foreign language. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with stammering speech]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **stammerings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with stammering]

Isaiah is using the word **tongue** to mean a foreign language, since the tongue is used for speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and with another language]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh himself will speak]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rest**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is a resting place]

Isaiah is using the adjective **weary** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to those who are weary]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **refreshing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [this refreshes]

This is the end of what Yahweh had said to the leaders. You may wish to mark the end of this speech with a closing quotation mark or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate the end of a quotation.

12.q: אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָמַ֣ר אֲלֵי⁠הֶ֗ם זֹ֤את הַ⁠מְּנוּחָה֙ הָנִ֣יחוּ לֶֽ⁠עָיֵ֔ף וְ⁠זֹ֖את הַ⁠מַּרְגֵּעָ֑ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א אָב֖וּא שְׁמֽוֹעַ
12.note: Isaiah uses the phrase **but they were not willing to hear** here to indicate a contrast between Yahweh’s offer of rest and refreshing and the leaders’ refusal to accept it. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [even though he said to them, “This is rest; give rest to the weary, and this is refreshing,” they were not willing to hear]

13.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the leaders were people who **stumble backward** and fall into traps. He means that because they rejected Yahweh’s word, they will experience defeat and captivity. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and face defeat and captivity]

The expression **be broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and collapse]

The expression **be ensnared** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and their enemies will ensnare them]

Because the leaders refused Yahweh’s offer of rest, his word will become for them mere repetitive sounds they cannot understand. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [As a result, the word of Yahweh will be]

Isaiah is using **men of mockery** as a common expression of the culture to mean “people who mock.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people who mock]

The leaders of Jerusalem are speaking of **Sheol** as if it were a living thing that could make an agreement. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we have made an agreement with those in Sheol]

Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The overwhelming military force]

The leaders of Jerusalem are speaking as if their deception were a physical **refuge** and a place where they have **hidden** themselves. Yahweh is using **Behold me, one has laid** as a common expression of this culture to mean “I am going to lay.” Someone using this expression would more commonly say “Behold me, laying.” Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making a solemn pronouncement. He is using the past tense to describe something that is going to happen in the future in order to show that this event will certainly happen. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am surely going to lay]

If your readers would not be familiar with what a **plumb line** is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. See the UST.

Alternate translation: [But his judgment will completely destroy the protection that their lies provided]

Alternate translation: [and Yahweh’s judgment will completely expose those who are hiding]

Yahweh is speaking of **Sheol** as if it were a living thing that could enter into an agreement that will not stand. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will not escape the realm of the dead]

The word translated as **when** indicates that two things happen at the same time. The **overflowing scourge passes through**, and at that same time, the leaders will be trampled by it. If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **agreement**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the matter about which you agreed]

19.note: Isaiah is repeating forms of the phrase **by morning** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. 21.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

21.q: כְ⁠הַר פְּרָצִים֙ יָק֣וּם יְהוָ֔ה כְּ⁠עֵ֖מֶק בְּ⁠גִבְע֣וֹן יִרְגָּ֑ז
21.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **Yahweh will arise as at Mount Perazim** and **he will rage as in the Valley of Gibeon** in past battles, so he will act powerfully now in judgment against his own people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will arise just as he did at Mount Perazim and will rage just as he did in the Valley of Gibeon]
The word **Mount Perazim** is the name of a place where Yahweh enabled David to defeat the Philistines (see 2 Samuel 5:20).

21.q: לַ⁠עֲשׂ֤וֹת מַעֲשֵׂ֨⁠הוּ֙ זָ֣ר מַעֲשֵׂ֔⁠הוּ וְ⁠לַֽ⁠עֲבֹד֙ עֲבֹ֣דָת֔⁠וֹ נָכְרִיָּ֖ה עֲבֹדָתֽ⁠וֹ
21.note: Isaiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [to accomplish his work—his strange work—and perform his deed—his foreign deed]

21.q: לַ⁠עֲשׂ֤וֹת מַעֲשֵׂ֨⁠הוּ֙ זָ֣ר מַעֲשֵׂ֔⁠הוּ וְ⁠לַֽ⁠עֲבֹד֙ עֲבֹ֣דָת֔⁠וֹ נָכְרִיָּ֖ה עֲבֹדָתֽ⁠וֹ
21.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of lines in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. The UST models one way to combine these lines. You could also use a different connecting word than **and** to show that the second line is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [to work his work—strange is his work—yes, to do his deed—foreign is his deed]

22.note: Isaiah uses the phrase **And now** to indicate a contrast between the leaders’ current mocking attitude and the serious judgment that is coming upon them. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Because of this]

The word **lest** marks **your bonds strengthen** as an outcome that Isaiah does not want to happen. He tells the leaders to stop mocking so that God will not punish them more severely. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [if you do not want your bonds to strengthen]
See how you translated the similar expression in 28:2.

The expression **is decreed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has decreed]

22.q: כִּֽי־כָלָ֨ה וְ⁠נֶחֱרָצָ֜ה שָׁמַ֗עְתִּי מֵ⁠אֵ֨ת אֲדֹנָ֧⁠י יְהוִ֛ה צְבָא֖וֹת עַל־כָּל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
22.note: Isaiah has been conveying Yahweh’s warning to the leaders, but now he briefly interjects his own testimony, **—I have heard from the Lord, Yahweh of Armies—**, to confirm the divine source of this message. If it would be helpful in your language, you could set this aside apart from the surrounding text. Alternate translation: [For destruction is decreed over all of the earth. I, Isaiah, have heard from the Lord, Yahweh of Armies.]

Isaiah says **over all of the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that the destruction will be extensive and devastating. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [over all the nations of the earth]

23.note: The terms **Listen** and **hear** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Listen attentively to]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [attend to me]

24.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the plowman. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Does the plowman open]

24.q: הֲ⁠כֹ֣ל הַ⁠יּ֔וֹם יַחֲרֹ֥שׁ הַ⁠חֹרֵ֖שׁ לִ⁠זְרֹ֑עַ יְפַתַּ֥ח וִֽ⁠ישַׂדֵּ֖ד אַדְמָתֽ⁠וֹ
24.note:
Isaiah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [A plowman is not plowing all of the day to sow!
He does not only open and harrow his ground!]

Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that a farmer does not keep breaking up the soil indefinitely. The expected answer is “no.” If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [He does not open and harrow his ground!]

25.q: הֲ⁠לוֹא֙ אִם־שִׁוָּ֣ה פָנֶ֔י⁠הָ וְ⁠הֵפִ֥יץ קֶ֖צַח וְ⁠כַמֹּ֣ן יִזְרֹ֑ק וְ⁠שָׂ֨ם חִטָּ֤ה שׂוֹרָה֙ וּ⁠שְׂעֹרָ֣ה נִסְמָ֔ן וְ⁠כֻסֶּ֖מֶת גְּבֻלָתֽ⁠וֹ
25.note: Isaiah is using the question form to make an assertion contrary to the suggestion he has just made in the previous verse. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No, he levels its face and scatters black cumin and sprinkle cumin and puts wheat in a row and barley in an appointed place and spelt at its border!]
See how you translated the term “Or” in [10:9](http://../10/09.md). Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

Isaiah is using **its face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “its surface.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he does not level its surface]
The pronoun **its** refers to the ground. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the ground’s face]

**Black cumin** is a kind of aromatic seed plant (Nigella sativa) used for flavoring food. If your readers would not be familiar with what **black cumin** is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [spice seeds]

The expression **appointed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in its proper place]

**Spelt** is a kind of grain similar to wheat. If your readers would not be familiar with what **spelt** is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and grain]

26.note: The pronoun **his** and the pronoun **him** refer to the farmer, while the pronoun **he** in the second clause refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [For the farmer’s God instructs him in judgment; God teaches him]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the right way]

27.note: A **sledge** is a kind of heavy wooden threshing tool dragged over grain to separate the seeds from the stalks. If your readers would not be familiar with what a **sledge** is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with a heavy threshing tool]

The expression **is the wheel of a cart rolled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [does the wheel of a cart roll]

The expression **is not threshed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [farmers do not thresh black cumin with a sledge]

The expression **is beaten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [farmers beat]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. The full meaning is that black cumin is beaten **with a stick**, and cumin is beaten **with a rod**. Alternate translation: [with a stick, and cumin is beaten with a rod]

28.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the farmer, and the pronoun **it** refers to the grain. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the farmer does not thresh the grain forever]

The expression **is crushed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A farmer crushes bread grain]

Isaiah is repeating forms of the verb **thresh** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [although the farmer certainly does not thresh it forever]

Isaiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between **drives the wheel of his cart over it** and **does not crush it**. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Although he drives the wheel of his cart over it, his horse does not crush it]

29.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wise people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wise things he says]
